text:
A starter that turns flat and sour has usually run out of food. Suppose you feed the wild yeast and lactobacilli once and then leave them on a 26°C counter for days. They use up the sugars in the flour within roughly 8–12 hours. After that, acid builds up faster than gas.

Lactic and acetic acids pull the pH below about 3.8. Yeast tolerates acid far less well than the bacteria living alongside it, so the yeast stalls. The bacteria keep souring the starter, but the bubbles stop.

Hooch is the grey layer of alcohol that pools on top. It means the culture has used up its food.

Two other causes are possible. Chlorinated tap water can bleach a young colony, and storage near 4°C slows fermentation to a crawl.

To fix it, discard most of the starter. Then feed it every twelve hours, at a ratio of 1:2:2 starter to flour to water. With fresh starch and less acid, the starter typically recovers and doubles again within two or three feedings.
